label: US Unemployment Rate
deltaNote: July 2026 (Aug 7): NFP fell 23,000 — a sharp miss vs the ~83,000 gain expected — with May and June revised down a combined 103,000. Unemployment eased to 4.1%, largely on lower labor-force participation rather than underlying strength. Markets read the report as reducing Fed hike risk; S&P 500 closed at a record high same day.

label: US PCE Inflation (May 2026 — Highest Since 2023)
deltaNote: MAY 2026 (released June 25): Headline PCE 4.1% YoY (+0.4% MoM) — highest since April 2023. Core PCE 3.4% YoY (vs 3.3% forecast). Personal income and spending each +0.7% MoM; saving rate held at 3%. Released just over a week after Warsh's hawkish dot plot, complicating the disinflation narrative even as Iran-deal oil relief began working through the data. June CPI (July 14) subsequently cooled to 3.5%, suggesting May PCE may mark the cycle high.

label: Fed Funds Rate
source: Federal Reserve FOMC, July 29 2026 (held; 3 hawkish dissents)
delta: Held at 3.50-3.75%; 3 dissents wanted a hike
deltaNote: July 28-29: FOMC held at 3.50-3.75% despite the July 23 oil-driven inflation scare that had pushed September hike odds to ~82%. Three members dissented in favor of a hike — Warsh called it a 'good family fight.' The Aug 7 jobs miss (NFP -23K) subsequently cooled hike expectations for September. AUG 12-17 UPDATE: A Reuters poll of 104 economists found 94 expect the Fed to hold at 3.50-3.75% in September and 80 see no change through year-end; market pricing implies roughly 70% odds of a September hold, though futures still price in one hike by December. The Aug 17 expiration of the US-Iran MOU (no deal) and the resulting oil/yield jump added modest upside risk to hike bets even as the underlying data flow favors a hold.

label: ECB Deposit Facility Rate
source: ECB Governing Council, June 11 2026 (25bp hike — first since July 2023)
deltaNote: June 11: ECB raised all three key rates 25bp — deposit facility to 2.25%, main refi to 2.40%, marginal lending to 2.65% (effective June 17). First hike since July 2023, reversing the final step of the prior 8-cut easing cycle. New staff projections: HICP 3.0% (2026)/2.3% (2027)/2.0% (2028); growth cut to 0.8%/1.2%/1.5%. Lagarde left the door open to further tightening.

label: US 10Y / 30Y Treasury Yield
source: CNBC / Federal Reserve H.15 / FRED; July 23 - August 17, 2026
delta: Round-tripped again: eased to 4.65% (10Y) on Aug 13's flat PPI, then jumped Aug 17 as the US-Iran MOU's 60-day window expired without a deal, reviving the oil-driven inflation premium alongside structurally rising long-end supply concerns.
deltaNote: AUG 14-17: The Aug 14 UAE tanker attacks and the Aug 17 expiration of the US-Iran MOU (Trump ruled out an extension) re-injected war-risk premium into oil (Brent ~$91) just as national debt concerns (nearing $40T) and stubborn above-target inflation kept long-end yields elevated. The 30-year Treasury yield rose to 5.31-5.32% on Aug 17 — its highest level since June 2007 — while the 10-year added to 4.72-4.74%. A Reuters poll of 104 economists (Aug 12-17) found 94 expect the Fed to hold at 3.50-3.75% in September, with market pricing near 70% odds of a hold, though futures still imply one hike by December.

deltaNote: May 2026: CB 93.1 (beat ~91.9 forecast; released May 26) — Present Situation Index 121.2 (down 3.2 pts); Expectations Index 74.4 (16th consecutive month below 80 recession-warning threshold). Two-thirds of consumers cutting spending due to inflation (highest proportion outside official recession). Michigan Final May 44.8 (all-time record low in 70+ year survey history).

label: Michigan Consumer Sentiment (August 2026 Preliminary)
deltaNote: AUG 2026 PRELIMINARY (released Aug 14): 51.0, badly missing the 54.5 consensus and down from July's final 55.2. Index of Consumer Expectations fell more sharply than Current Conditions; short-term expectations -11%, long-term projections -17%. Only 8% of consumers expect income growth to outpace inflation. Year-ahead inflation expectations rose to 4.3%. Sentiment fell across demographic and political lines, sharpest among Republicans, older consumers, lower-income households, and those without college degrees. Still well above May 2026's all-time record low of 44.8, but the renewed slide — alongside July retail sales' steepest drop in over a year (Aug 14) — marks the clearest crack yet in the 'resilient consumer' narrative. Final August reading due Aug 28.

label: S&P 500 / Market Risk Gauge

source: CNBC / TheStreet / Yahoo Finance / Federal Reserve; July 23 – August 17, 2026
delta: Round trip continues: the fresh Aug 13 record (7,799, first close above 7,800 intraday) gave way to a two-day pullback — the Aug 14 retail-sales/sentiment miss, then an Aug 17 slide (Dow -0.5%, S&P -0.5%, Nasdaq -0.3%) as the US-Iran MOU expired and oil/yields jumped together.
deltaNote: JULY 23-AUG 17 ARC: Oil-driven hike fears triggered the sharpest selloff of the window July 23. The FOMC's July 29 hold, the Aug 7 jobs shock, and Aug 12-13's cooling CPI/PPI prints drove a rally to a fresh S&P record (7,799) on Aug 13. That reversed over the following days: the Aug 14 retail-sales/sentiment miss, a second Hormuz tanker attack, and finally the Aug 17 expiration of the US-Iran MOU (no deal, no extension) pushed Brent to ~$91 and the 30-year Treasury yield to 5.31-5.32% — highest since 2007 — pulling stocks off their highs even as September hike odds remain low (Reuters poll: 94/104 economists expect a hold).

label: US Avg Effective Tariff Rate
value: Section 301 Forced-Labor Tariffs (10-12.5%) on 60 Economies Live Since Jul 24; Canada Section 338 Tariffs (50% on ~$20B) Due at Midnight Aug 19
source: USTR / Global Trade Alert / Holland & Knight; CP24 / CBC / BNN Bloomberg; July 24 - August 18, 2026
contestNote: The Section 122 tariff surcharge expired by statute at 12:01am EDT July 24; USTR's Section 301 forced-labor tariffs (10% or 12.5%, 60 economies) took effect the same minute, avoiding a coverage gap. Canada/Mexico USMCA-qualifying goods and CAFTA-DR textiles remain exempt from Section 301 — but the separate Section 338 threat on Canada (50% tariffs on ~$20B of autos, alcohol, and dairy) is due at 12:01am EDT Aug 19 absent a deal. Carney spoke with Trump by phone Aug 17, calling talks 'very intense and delicate'; LeBlanc met USTR Greer and Commerce Secretary Lutnick in Washington the same day (4th meeting in 3 weeks) saying 'our job is not yet done.' Sticking points: auto-tariff content rules, steel/aluminum tariffs, and dairy supply management.

Three July typhoons disrupted manufacturing hubs and fading subsidy support weighed on durable-goods spending. Beijing's late-July Politburo pledge of 'targeted stimulus' has yet to translate into major new measures.

label: Global Policy Uncertainty / Recession Risk
value: AUG 17: US-Iran MOU Expires Without a Deal, 30Y Yield Hits 5.31% (Highest Since 2007); China July Activity Data Misses; Canada Faces 50% Tariffs at Midnight Aug 19
source: Federal Reserve / BEA / BLS / China NBS / Census Bureau / U. Michigan; July 17 – August 18, 2026
delta: AUG 14-18 ARC — CONSUMER CRACKS, THEN GEOPOLITICAL AND BOND-MARKET STRESS: The Aug 14 retail-sales miss and Michigan sentiment collapse pulled stocks off their Aug 13 record. Aug 17 brought two compounding shocks: the US-Iran MOU's 60-day window expired without a deal (Trump ruled out an extension), pushing Brent to ~$91 and driving the 30-year Treasury yield to 5.31-5.32% — highest since June 2007 — while China's July activity data missed across output, retail sales, and investment. Aug 18 added a fresh trade-policy cliff: Carney and Trump spoke by phone hours before 50% Section 338 tariffs on ~$20B of Canadian goods are due to take effect at midnight, with talks still 'very intense and delicate.'
deltaNote: AUG 18 RECESSION RISK SNAPSHOT: Four distinct risk channels are now flashing simultaneously — a bond market pricing in structurally higher long-end yields on debt/inflation concerns, a reignited Iran war-risk premium in oil, a deepening China slowdown, and an imminent US-Canada tariff deadline. None individually rises to a 2026-recession-defining shock, but the simultaneity is new. Next catalysts: the Aug 19 Section 338 deadline, the final August Michigan sentiment reading (Aug 28), and the September 16-17 FOMC meeting.

label: BOJ Policy Rate
source: Bank of Japan, June 16 2026 (25bp hike — highest since 1995)
deltaNote: June 16: BOJ hiked 25bp to 1.00%, the highest level since 1995, in a 7-1 vote (Asada dissenting) — citing Iran-war energy-cost pass-through risk. The hike landed the same day Warsh's first FOMC opened, raising August-2024-style carry-unwind concerns; the immediate market reaction was orderly (Nikkei +0.46%), but the yen still fell to a fresh 40-year low past 162/USD by June 30 despite the hike and an estimated $72.5bn in prior FX intervention.
